title: Blockchain and the Ecosystem
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/title: Mining, Proof of Work and Proof of Stake
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/0/body: Transactions are grouped into **blocks**, and each block is chained to the one before it. On Bitcoin, **miners** compete to build the next block, and the winner gets the **block reward** plus the **transaction fees**. On average, a new block is made every **10 minutes**.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/0/tip: To change an old transaction, you'd have to rebuild every block after it too. That's why a blockchain is practically unchangeable.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/1/body: In **Proof of Work (PoW)**, miners use special machines to make trillions of guesses per second until a math puzzle is solved. This eats up a lot of **electricity and hardware**, and that cost is exactly what makes cheating so expensive. **Bitcoin** uses Proof of Work.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: On the Bitcoin network, what does the miner who builds a new block get?
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/2/options/0: The block reward plus transaction fees
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/2/options/2: A cut of exchange trading volume
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/2/options/3: A vote to change Bitcoin's price
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/2/explanation: Each block's winning miner gets freshly minted bitcoin (the block reward) plus the fees from every transaction in that block.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/3/statement: In Proof of Work, a miner with more computing power (hashrate) has a better chance of building the next block.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/3/explanation: Mining is like a lottery, and every guess is a ticket. Stronger hardware means more tickets: better odds, but no guaranteed win.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/4/body: In **Proof of Stake (PoS)**, instead of electricity, the **network's coin is locked up as collateral** (staked). **Validators** confirm blocks and earn rewards; if they cheat, part of their collateral gets **slashed**. **Ethereum** switched to Proof of Stake in September 2022.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: With this switch (The Merge), Ethereum's energy use dropped by more than 99%.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/5/pairs/2/mea: Penalty on a cheating validator's stake
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/6/sentence: In Proof of Work, miners spend ___ and hardware; in Proof of Stake, validators lock up coins as ___.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/6/explanation: PoW's security comes from the real cost of electricity and hardware. PoS's security comes from collateral that cheaters lose.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/7/prompt: On a Proof of Stake network, a validator tries to approve a fake transaction and the network catches it. What most likely happens to them?
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/7/options/0: Part of their stake gets slashed
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/7/options/3: Their hashrate goes to other miners
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/7/explanation: In PoS, cheating hits the validator's own pocket: part of their staked coins gets burned or taken away.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/8/statement: Like Ethereum, Bitcoin now uses Proof of Stake too.
lessons/crypto-u2-l1/steps/8/explanation: Bitcoin is still Proof of Work, and miners build blocks with special machines (ASICs). It was Ethereum that moved to Proof of Stake in 2022.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/0/body: Bitcoin was built mainly to **send and store value**, but **Ethereum** is a programmable blockchain. It can run **smart contracts**: code stored on the blockchain that **runs automatically** once its conditions are met.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/0/tip: Every transaction and contract on Ethereum is paid for in ETH. This fee is called "gas".
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/prompt: What exactly is a smart contract?
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/options/0: Code that runs automatically on a blockchain
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/options/1: A paper contract signed by an exchange
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/options/2: A cheap kind of hardware wallet
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/options/3: An app for buying coins fast
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/1/explanation: A smart contract is a program that lives on the blockchain and runs exactly as coded, with no middleman. A decentralized exchange is one example.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/2/body: A **coin** is the native currency of its own blockchain, like BTC on Bitcoin or ETH on Ethereum. A **token** is built with a smart contract on another network's blockchain. For example, **USDT** exists as a token on both Ethereum and Tron.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/3/statement: To move an ERC-20 token (like Tether on Ethereum), you need a little ETH in that same wallet.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/3/explanation: Every transaction fee on Ethereum is paid in ETH, even if what you're moving is Tether.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/4/pairs/3/mea: Fee to run an Ethereum transaction
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/5/body: A **standard** means all tokens speak one common language: a wallet that understands ERC-20 supports **thousands of tokens**. Regular tokens are **fungible**, so every unit is the same as any other, but each **NFT** is one of a kind.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/6/prompt: Which one counts as a "coin", not a "token"?
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/6/explanation: ETH is Ethereum's own native currency. The other options were built with smart contracts on Ethereum, so they're tokens.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/7/sentence: ETH is the native ___ of the Ethereum network, but USDT on Ethereum is a ___.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/7/explanation: A coin belongs to the blockchain itself and pays its fees; a token is built on top of another network's blockchain.
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/prompt: A friend pitches a new token and says, "It's built on Ethereum, so it must be safe." What do you think?
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/options/0: Making a token is easy; the blockchain doesn't make a project safe
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/options/1: True; the Ethereum team approves every token
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/options/2: True; Ethereum tokens never lose their value
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/options/3: It's only safe if it costs under a dollar
lessons/crypto-u2-l2/steps/8/explanation: Anyone can create an ERC-20 token with a few lines of code. The blockchain just records transactions; checking a project's quality and honesty is up to you.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/0/body: **Market cap = price × circulating supply.** This number shows what a whole coin is worth, and when comparing projects it matters far more than the price of one unit.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/1/prompt: Which coin has the bigger market cap?
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/1/explanation: 0.01 × 100 billion = $1 billion, and 50 × 4 million = $200 million. A lower price doesn't mean a coin is smaller or cheaper.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/2/statement: A coin priced under 1 cent can reach $10 more easily than others, because it's cheap.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/2/explanation: If a coin with a supply of 100 billion hit $10, its market cap would be $1,000 billion (one trillion)! Measure growth by market cap, not unit price.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/3/body: **Dominance** is Bitcoin's share of the **total crypto market cap**. If Bitcoin's market cap is $1.2 trillion and the whole market is $2 trillion, dominance is **60%**.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/4/prompt: The total crypto market cap is $3 trillion and Bitcoin's market cap is $1.5 trillion. What is Bitcoin's dominance?
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/4/explanation: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5, so half of the whole crypto market's value belongs to Bitcoin.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/5/body: When **dominance rises**, Bitcoin's share grows: either more money flowed into it or altcoins fell harder. When it **falls**, altcoins have taken a bigger share. Many traders use this chart to follow money moving between Bitcoin and alts.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/6/prompt: This is a Bitcoin dominance chart (in percent). What can you take from it?
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/6/options/3/l: The total crypto market is flat
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/6/explanation: Dominance went from about 58% to 52%, so alts gained share against Bitcoin. This chart only shows relative share; on its own, it doesn't tell you whether Bitcoin's price went up or down.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/7/prompt: In one month, Bitcoin's price rose 10%, but its dominance fell from 55% to 50%. What does that mean?
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/7/options/0: Altcoins as a group grew faster than Bitcoin
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/7/options/1: Altcoins fell and only Bitcoin grew
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/7/explanation: Bitcoin got bigger but its share shrank, so the rest of the market must have grown faster. With these numbers, altcoins' market cap grew by about 34%.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/8/sentence: You get market cap by multiplying ___ by ___.
lessons/crypto-u2-l3/steps/8/explanation: Market cap uses circulating supply. If you multiply price by max supply, you get a different number called FDV.
